description:
Dreamworld to Earth. Do you copy?

We’re two sisters from Dreamworld, and we’re agents with NHorizon. When a mission sounds a little impossible, we like to find out exactly why.

For our latest assignment, Mission: Ripple, we’ve sent the mission brief to Snowy, who oversees space missions at nHorizon. Snowy will brief you before launch. Once you’re in the pilot’s seat, the choices are yours.

We love design, science, and ideas that are just weird enough to work!
summary:
Welcome to Sleeping Observatory! Have you ever wondered why something can seem perfect, but still end up failing?
This can happen in space missions, too. Even if every part of a spacecraft works perfectly, it doesn't always mean the mission will succeed. Every decision can affect other parts of the mission, and even a small choice can change the final result.
That's why we created Mission: Ripple!
In our interactive game, players become part of a space mission design team and work with four Dreamlings to complete a mission. Players choose scientific instruments, orbits, launch vehicles, and other equipment while managing limited resources like budget, mass, power, and communication.
The most special part of our game is the Ripple Effect. It shows how one decision can affect other systems. By testing their mission, making changes, and comparing results, players can discover better solutions.
Through this game, we hope to make space mission design more interesting and easier to understand. We want players to realize that a successful mission isn't about having the best equipment, but about making everything work together.
details:
MISSION: RIPPLE

Our Project Solution

Mission: Ripple is an interactive web game designed to help players understand the challenges of planning a space mission.

We wanted to make space engineering more interesting and easier to understand, especially for people who have never explored spacecraft design before. Instead of only reading about spacecraft systems, players can make their own decisions, test different designs, and see how their choices affect the mission.

In our game, players work with four Dreamlings, each responsible for a different part of mission planning. They must make decisions about scientific instruments, spacecraft systems, launch services, and communication while managing limited resources.

Our main idea is that choosing the best equipment for one system does not always create the best mission overall.

Caption: Welcome to Mission: Ripple, an interactive space mission design game.

How Our Game Works

When players enter Mission: Ripple, they meet four Dreamlings:

  • Lumi — Science: Focuses on scientific goals and instruments.
  • Orin — Engineering: Works with spacecraft systems and resources.
  • Tera — Launch: Considers launch options and limitations.
  • Nova — Operations: Focuses on communication and mission operations.

Each Dreamling has a different responsibility, but they are all working toward the same mission goal.

Players visit their workstations and select different equipment and systems. Every option has its own advantages and limitations, so players need to consider factors such as budget, mass, power, and data requirements.

Caption: Players make decisions about different mission systems while managing limited resources.

After completing their design, players run a mission simulation.

The simulation checks whether the selected systems meet the mission requirements and shows whether the mission succeeds or fails.

For example, a successful mission shows that the required science data was delivered to Earth. If something goes wrong, the results explain which requirements were not met.

Players can then return to their workstations, adjust their choices, and try again.

What Makes Our Game Different?

Our favorite feature is the Ripple Effect.

We wanted to show that space mission design is not simply about choosing the most powerful or expensive equipment.

For example, a more advanced scientific instrument might collect better data, but it could also require more electricity and generate more information.

If the spacecraft cannot provide enough power, the instrument may not work as planned. Even if the spacecraft collects the data, the mission could still fail if the communication system cannot transmit the required information to Earth within the available contact time.

This is why we named our game Mission: Ripple.

Just like ripples spreading across water, one decision can create consequences across several connected systems.

Instead of only telling players that their mission failed, we wanted them to understand why it failed and what they could change.

Caption: The mission simulation shows how a problem in one system can affect the entire mission.

The Science Behind Our Game

We researched NASA educational and engineering resources, including Design and Develop Science Missions and NASA's Mission Design Lab, to understand how real space missions are planned.

We learned that designing a mission involves more than choosing scientific instruments. Engineers must also consider spacecraft mass, electrical power, communication, launch limitations, available resources, and scientific goals.

These factors are connected, and changing one part of a mission can affect other parts.

We used these engineering concepts to create the rules behind our simulation. For example, the game checks whether the selected systems fit within resource limits and whether the communication system can support the mission's data requirements.

Our simulation uses simplified educational calculations rather than actual NASA spacecraft specifications. Its purpose is to demonstrate engineering trade-offs, not to predict the performance of a real NASA mission.

Caption: A successful simulation shows that the mission requirements have been met.

How We Created It + Artificial Intelligence

We developed Mission: Ripple as an interactive browser-based game.

Creative development: Our team worked together on the core ideas, mission concept, story, characters, gameplay ideas, and design decisions.

We created Snowy and the four Dreamlings to make the game more welcoming and interesting than a traditional science lesson.

Each Dreamling represents a different part of mission planning, helping players understand why different engineering decisions need to work together.

We used several tools during development:

  • ChatGPT: Assisted with coding, troubleshooting, background music, and improving the game's implementation.
  • Runway: Helped create introductory visuals (intro) and animation.
  • Netlify: Used to publish and host our interactive game website.

AI helped us develop the project, but our team was responsible for its creative direction and final decisions.

Additional Game Features

Besides the main mission simulation, we also added several features to make our game easier and more fun to play.

Five Languages: Players can switch between English, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Spanish in Settings. We wanted people from different countries to be able to understand and enjoy our game.

Multiplayer Mode: Our game also has a multiplayer beta where up to four players can join the same room using a room code. Each player chooses a Dreamling and is responsible for their own workstation. They can see what their teammates are doing, but only change their own decisions. This makes communication and teamwork an important part of the game.

Settings and About: Players can change some visual settings, such as turning off twinkling stars or reducing animation. The About section explains the background of our mission, what players need to do, and the different roles of the four Dreamlings.

Single-Player Mode: Players can also complete the mission by themselves, switching between the four Dreamlings to make decisions for each system. This way, they can still experience the whole game without needing a team.

We reviewed and adjusted the results throughout development to make the game work the way we wanted.

Project Impact

General Impact

Mission: Ripple encourages critical thinking, teamwork, and problem-solving.

Players experiment with different choices, observe their consequences, and improve their designs when something goes wrong.

The game also introduces systems thinking, which means understanding how different parts of a larger system depend on one another.

Teens and Students

For younger players, the game offers an approachable introduction to space engineering. We hope it encourages more students to become interested in science, engineering, and space exploration.

Adults

For adults, the game offers an opportunity to practice making decisions with limited resources and understanding how one choice can affect a larger system.

Educators

Teachers could potentially use the game to introduce engineering trade-offs, spacecraft systems, and discussions about how complicated problems are solved.

Our Goal and Limitations

Our goal is to make space mission design more understandable and accessible to people with different levels of scientific knowledge.

We want players to experience how engineers think about a mission, rather than only learning the names of spacecraft components.

However, our game is an educational simulation, not professional mission-design software.

The resource values and calculations are simplified, and the game does not represent every technical challenge involved in planning a real spacecraft mission.

The challenges we met is that, when we put all the AI-generated videos together, it was not smoothly as we expected, and it is difficult to combine all the sources together.

In the future, we hope to add more mission scenarios, engineering choices, and opportunities for players to explore different solutions.

Most importantly, we want players to understand that complicated problems do not always have one perfect answer.

Sometimes, success depends on understanding how everything works together.

Tools and Technologies Used

Game Development: Interactive browser-based game with AI-assisted coding and troubleshooting.

Website Hosting: Netlify, used to publish our game online.

Animation: Runway, used for introductory visuals and animation.

Scientific Research: NASA educational and mission-design resources.

Creative Design: Original mission concept, story, characters, and gameplay decisions developed by our team.
